Republic of the Philippines DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT A. Francisco Gold Condominium II Bldg, EDSA corner Mapagmahal St., Diliman, Quezon City 22 April 2010 LEGAL SERVICE DILG OPINION NO. 58 s. 2010 MS. GUILLERMA G. DE PAULA State Auditor III Team Leader COMISSION ON AUDIT Cluster IV- Visayas Local Government Sector Sub-Cluster III-Team 8 Dear Ms. De Paula: This has reference to your earlier letter requesting for a legal opinion on 'whether the City of Kabankalan can act as Co-Ob/igor of Kabankalan Water District (KWD)' in obtaining a loan of Fifteen Million Pesos (PhP 15,000,000.00) with the Development Bank of the Philippines (DBP), and where such loan is secured by a continuing assignment with hold-out provision of the City of Kabankalan's applicable portion of its Internal Revenue Allotment (IRA)I. Records will show that of the four (4) prior indorsements2 before your query reached this Department, there were conflicting views as to the propriety of the abovementioned act of the City Government of Kabankalan and that of IRA being used as security or collateral. 3 In threshing out the issues, COA State Auditor Maria Gleda E. Lim opined that "the City of Kabankalan has the legal capacity to sign the agreement", recommending further that the said "City Government executed a separate memorandum of agreement with Kabankalan City Water District for the IRA assigned as holdout of the loan". On the other hand, COA Cluster Director Delfin P. Aguilar had an opposing view in his 2nd Indorsement, stating among others that "the resulting exposure and contingent liability may be disadvantageous to the City" as the latter is not acting as the Lender but a Co-Obligor. 2 3 Page 1, Deed of Assignment with Hold-Out and Page 5, Term Loan Agreement State Auditor V Maria Glenda E. Lim (ISt and 3rd Indorsements), Cluster Director Delfin P. Aguilar (2nd Indorsement), and Regional Cluster Director Atty. Viola P. Villanueva, Regional Legal and Adjudication Office (4th Indorsement) ISt and 3rd Indorsement

City Mayor Pedro P. Zayco Jr., in his letter dated 02 January 2007, justified his acts by claiming that KWD initially sought the PhP 15.0 Million loan from the City Government of Kabankalan primarily to finance KWD's Filtration System Project using the Hilabangan River, and ultimately provide a potable water system in Kabankalan, said to be a major problem of the city. Instead of granting the loan, the City Government of Kabankalan eventually entered into a loan agreement with the DBP, with the City Government as a guarantor/co-obligor of KWD, the principal debtor or obligor in the said agreement. While City Mayor Zayco Jr. admitted assigning a portion of the Kabankalan City's IRA as security, he also mentioned that it entered into a Memorandum of Agreement4 with KWD to ensure its faithful compliance to the loan. In resolving the conflicting views, we are of the opinion that a local government unit thru its chief executive can enter into a contract, obtain a loan agreement or create indebtedness, and utilize a portion of its IRA to finance or fund development projects necessary for the effective delivery of the basic services to its constituents, subject to certain conditions provided under the law. Within their respective territorial jurisdictions, local government units shall ensure and promote the general welfare of its inhabitants or 5 It shall endeavor to be self-reliant, and is mandated to constituents. exercise such other functions and responsibilities as are necessary, appropriate, or incidental to efficient and effective provisions of the basic services and facilities6. In the exercise of its powers in conformity with the law, a local As such, it government unit is a body politic and a corporate entity. performs dual functions, governmental and proprietary. Governmental functions are those that concern the health, safety and the advancement of the public good or welfare as affecting the public generally. Proprietary functions are those that seek to obtain special corporate benefits or earn pecuniary profit and intended for private advantage and benefit. When exercising governmental powers and performing governmental duties, an LGU is an agency of the national government. When engaged in corporate activities, it acts as an agent of the community in the administration of local affairs. 4 5 6 7 8 Executed on 01 March 2006 which provides that in the event of KWD's failure to comply with the terms and conditions of the loan agreement with DBP, whatever amount the DBP deducts from the City Government shall be deducted or offset from the latter's water bills with KWD Section 16 on General Welfare, Local Government Code (LGC) Section 17, LGC Section 15, LGC Republic of the Philippines vs The City of Davao, G.R. No. 148622, 12 September 2002 2

The authority of the local chief executive to enter into a contract is sanctioned by Section 22 (a)(5) and (c) in relation to Section 455 (b) (1) (vi) of the Local Government Code of 1991 [Republic Act No. 7160] CCode' for brevity) , and we quote: "Section 22. Corporate Powers. - (a) Every local government unit, as a corporation, shall have the following powers: xxxx (5) To enter into contracts• and (c) Unless otherwise provided in this Code, no contract may be entered into executive in behalf of the local government unit without prior authorization by the sanggunian concerned. xxx Section 455. Chief Executive; Powers, Duties and Compensation. xxxx (b) For efficient, effective and economical governance the purpose of wllicll is the general welfare of the city and its inhabitants pursuant to Section 16 of this Code, the city mayor shall: (1) Exercise general supervision and control over all programs, projects, services, and activities of the city government. and in this connection, shall: xxxx (vi) Represent the city in all its business transactions and sign in its behalf all bonds, contracts and and such other obligations, documents upon authority of the panlungsod sangguniang pursuant to law or ordinance;" (emphasis and underscoring supplied) Further, Sections 295 up to 300 of the Code9 allows LGUs to create indebtedness and enter into credit and other financial transaction, 9 Title IV, Credit Financing 3

and upon Sanggunian approval, to jointly and severally contract loans, credits and other forms of indebtedness. Thus, to address the needs, promote general welfare, and ensure the effective delivery of the basic services to the people, a local government unit enjoys autonomy under the law. Anent the use of the IRA as a security or collateral, the same has been a permissive practice among the LGUs primarily to finance or fund developmental projects. IRA is intended, among others, to augment local resources to ensure that the minimum level of basic services is delivered to the LGUs' constituents. Section 287 of the same Code provides for the restriction on the use of IRA by the local government unit which is mandated to appropriate in its annual budget no less than twenty percent (20%) of its annual internal revenue allotment for development projects. To cite an example, the Housing and Urban Development Council has issued a primer entitled, 'LGU's Guidebook for Local Housing Project/Program'10 wherein 20% of IRA is stipulated as one of the acceptable collaterals from an LGU. While there is no particular statute or law that clearly defines, limits or restricts IRA-backed loans, an LGU is admonished to exercise prudence and strict compliance to the existing laws governing the use of IRA for developmental projects. We hope that the foregoing addressed your concerns with clarity. Very truly yours, By Authority of the Secretary: ATTY. JESUS B.
